title: The Arm It Really Is: Calibrating the Table From Measured Tool Positions, What a Measurement Cannot Tell Apart, and How Many Poses Are Enough

questions.question: Why is the arm on the bench not its table?
options: The table is rounded to too few digits
The controller adds its own offsets
Links and joint zeros are made to a tolerance, and every error is in the tool
questions.explanation: Each link length, twist and zero is made to a tolerance. A third of a degree at the shoulder, a metre from the tool, is millimetres there.

questions.question: After calibrating, the error on poses it had not seen was:
questions.explanation: Fitted to 60 poses measured to 0.05 mm, the table predicted 30 other poses to 0.100 mm, where the uncorrected one was 3.39 mm out.

questions.question: Fitted to only 4 poses, the error on others was:
options: 0.00000000 mm, as on its own poses
0.83 mm, though it was 0.00000000 mm on its own
questions.explanation: Four poses give 12 equations for 24 corrections, so they can be matched exactly without the arm being right. Elsewhere the error was 0.83 mm.

questions.question: Moving joint 2's offset or joint 3's by 1 mm gave tool places that differed by:
questions.explanation: Their axes are parallel, so a shift along either is the same shift of the tool. No set of poses can tell the two apart.

questions.question: What is the test of a calibration?
options: Its error on poses it was not fitted to
questions.explanation: A fit can always do well on what it was fitted to. Poses held back show whether it found the arm or only matched the data.

questions.question: Why do the fitted corrections not have to be the true ones?
options: Some give the same tool place whatever the joints do, so the measurements cannot separate them
questions.explanation: Along parallel axes two corrections have the same effect. The fit gets the tool's place right and the split between them is arbitrary.
